title: Complementary colours — Image Wiki
text:
Complementary colours
  The pair of colours that cancel each other. There are two different pairs answering to that name — the one that mixes to grey and the one your eye pairs — and they are almost never the same colour.

  
    Termcomplementary colours
    Also calledcomplements, opposite colours, visual complements, mixing complements, afterimage colour
    Not the same asmixing complements vs visual complements, complementary colours vs the complementary scheme, complement vs contrast
    Read10 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Two things called complementaryWhy each pair cancelsTwo things you can do with thisWhat the pair actually gives youCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Stare at a road sign in strong sun, then look at the pale wall beside it. A ghost of the sign floats there in the wrong colour — a red sign leaves a blue-green ghost.
That ghost is a complementary colour, and it is free evidence, produced by your own eye, that hues come in cancelling pairs. Painters have used the fact since the eighteenth century. The naturalist Buffon reported complementary coloured shadows and complementary afterimages to the French Academy of Sciences in 1742.
Then somebody wrote a textbook and flattened two different facts into one word. Mixing two paints to a grey and staring at a patch until it flips are not the same operation, and they do not name the same partner.
Two things called complementary
Pick out the definitions and there are three, not one:

Mixing complements — two paints, dyes or inks that can be mixed in some proportion to make a grey. Usually not a true flat-reflectance neutral, but something that looks grey.
Additive complements — two single wavelengths of light that mix to white.
Visual complements — two colours at opposite ends of a straight line drawn through the neutral centre of a perceptual hue plane. This is the pair your eye pairs, and the one the afterimage shows you.

Handprint's finding after measuring ninety pigments is blunt: visual and mixing complements are almost never the same colour. The visual complement of ultramarine blue is a yellowish green; its mixing complement is a dull deep yellow. Mix ultramarine with a greenish yellow and you do not get grey, you get a dark bluish green.

greyviridianPG18quinacridonemagentaPR122Visual complement: one huethe hue the eye pairs it with — theafterimage colour, straight through greyviridianPG18where the visualcomplement sitsmaroon endred orange endMixing complements: eight paintsevery one of them greys viridian out, andnone of them is the hue opposite it

The same paint, viridian, on both circles. Distance from the centre is chroma, so the dull viridian plots well inside the rim.
Left, its visual complement: quinacridone magenta, at hue 348° against viridian's 168°. Exactly one hue qualifies, because the definition is geometric.
Right, the paints that actually grey viridian out. Handprint lists eight — red brown, maroon, carmine, deep red, light and dark middle red, scarlet, red orange — spread across a 28° fan and none of them at 348°. Several are also mixing complements of turquoise paints. The dashed ring marks where the visual complement sat. Mixing complements do not pick out a hue; they pick out a shortlist.


That is why you cannot build a wheel out of them. Joy Turner Luke, writing the notes to the New Munsell Student Color Set, states it flatly: it is impossible to make a subtractive colour wheel where every colour mixed with its opposite gives grey.
Why each pair cancels
Mixing complements cancel because of what subtractive mixture does. A mixture reflects only the light that both ingredients reflect separately — so if their reflectance curves are roughly inverse, between them they absorb across the whole spectrum, and almost nothing chromatic gets out.

050100reflectance %400500600700wavelength, nmthe sameblue paint×red orangeearth colour=near neutralchroma 7Mixing complementsthe warm partner reflects almost no green,so the mixture has nothing left to reflect050100reflectance %400500600700wavelength, nmthe sameblue paint×greenishyellow=dull greenchroma 54Visual complementsboth partners reflect green strongly,so green survives the multiplication

Reflectance against wavelength, with the shaded band showing the mixture, modelled as the product of the two curves. The blue is identical in both panels; only its partner changes. The swatches are computed from the curves, not chosen by hand.
Left, a red-orange earth colour: it reflects nothing in the green, the blue reflects nothing in the red, and the product collapses. Chroma falls to 7 — a near-neutral, and a very dark one.
Right, the greenish yellow that is the blue's visual complement. Both partners reflect green strongly, so green survives the multiplication and comes out at chroma 54. To drag that back to neutral you must shift the warm partner toward red — which is exactly why the mixing complement sits redder than the visual one.


If you paint, the shortlist collapses to three rules worth remembering. Yellows from lemon up to a deep hansa yellow will not neutralise any cool pigment at all — they just make dull greens. Every blue, from violet-blue to teal, neutralises with something between deep yellow and middle red, and a dull earth colour does it better than an intense one. Every green neutralises with something between deep red and violet.
Visual complements cancel somewhere else entirely: in the wiring. Colour is carried on two opponent channels, one running violet-red against blue-green, the other yellow against blue-violet. Adapt one end of a channel and the channel rebounds toward the other end. So the afterimage of red is cyan-ish because red and blue-green are the two directions of one signal, and nothing about paint is involved.
Which of the two you want depends on what you are doing. If you are trying to knock a colour down without muddying it, you want the mixing complement, and you want it off a table rather than off a wheel. If you are deciding what to put next to what, the mixing relationships are invisible to a viewer — nobody can tell from a finished picture whether that grey came from two paints or twenty — so the visual complements are the ones that matter.
Two things you can do with this

stare at the white dot,saturated redL* 53, chroma 104, hue 40°then at the black oneplain whitewhat swims into view, roughly:hue 220°, and much paler than the patchRed gives blue greenstare at the white dot,saturated greenL* 60, chroma 68, hue 147°then at the black oneplain whitewhat swims into view, roughly:hue 327°, and much paler than the patchGreen gives magenta

Do it now, on this page. Fix your eye on the white dot for a slow count of twenty, then move to the black dot and blink once.
Red gives a blue green at hue 220°; green gives a magenta at 327°. In each case the ghost lands about 180° from the patch — that is the visual complement, and no wheel had to tell you.
Two honest limits. The ghost is far paler than the swatch shown here: Handprint measured afterimages as much lighter and much less saturated than their stimulus, so the pairing is not symmetrical. And it is not even around the circle — a saturated red throws an intense blue-green, but a saturated blue throws a feeble yellow.


The second method needs no eyestrain. Work in a perceptual space instead of on a wheel. In an editor's Lab mode you can fix the lightness and move around the neutral point to change hue while chroma and lightness hold still — David Briggs describes exactly this procedure. Read the hue angle of your starting colour, add 180, and match lightness and chroma. That gives you the visual complement with the other two dials pinned, which no printed wheel can do. Note the trap Briggs flags: desaturating in Lab preserves lightness, desaturating in plain RGB does not.
What the pair actually gives you
Not one effect. Handprint's own list of complementary contrasts: purple against green is almost restful, orange against cerulean cheerful, yellow against ultramarine stark, and spectrum red against greenish blue downright hostile. He calls that last pairing the most intense chromatic antagonism in the colour space.


Restful: violet-blue against green, Irises, 1889
Hostile: red against green, The Zouave, 1888


Left: Vincent van Gogh, Irises, 1889, J. Paul Getty Museum. Right: Vincent van Gogh, The Zouave, 1888, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam. Both public domain. One painter, one year apart, two complementary pairs.
Irises is violet-blue against green, and it settles. Nothing in it is very chromatic: the violet petals measure about chroma 38, the leaves 26, the yellow-green band at the top 39, and nothing exceeds 39. The green family covers roughly 37 per cent of the canvas to the blues' 23, and the two interleave as hundreds of leaf edges rather than meeting along one line.
The Zouave is red against green, and it will not settle. Follow the edge of the fez against the flat green wall. Sampled either side, the two are almost the same lightness — L* in the low twenties to low thirties on both — at almost the same chroma, 34 to 48. Equal value, equal strength, one hard boundary: neither colour can become the background, so the edge buzzes. The cap is about 5 per cent of the frame and it dominates a wall four times its size.


So a "complementary pair" is not a decision. It leaves lightness, chroma and relative area open, and those settle what you get.


Decorative: yellow against blue, Café Terrace at Night, 1888
Stark: the same pair, The Sower, 1888


Vincent van Gogh, Café Terrace at Night (Kröller-Müller Museum) and The Sower (Kröller-Müller Museum), both 1888, both public domain. Now the pair is held constant — yellow against blue-violet in both — and only the handling changes.
In the Café Terrace the two are near-matched in strength: the awning and lit wall run about chroma 47, the night sky about 36, and the warm areas take 30 per cent of the canvas to the sky's 19. Read the cobbles: gold and blue strokes alternate all the way down, so the two hues are woven rather than opposed. Decorative, not tense.
In The Sower the same hue pair is unbalanced on purpose. The sky reaches chroma 60 while the ploughed field sits near 25, and the field is shattered into blue, lilac and orange flecks that average out. One side is loud and whole, the other quiet and broken. Stark, from the same two hues.


Common mistakes

"Complements mix to grey." Only mixing complements, only approximately, and the neutral you get is usually very dark. Visual complements mixed together give you a dull version of whatever they have in common — often a green.
"There is one complement of red." There is one visual complement. There is a shortlist of mixing complements, and it changes with the brand of paint and the medium.
"Darken a colour by adding its complement." Briggs tested it: for some colours it works for a little way and then pulls the mixture off course; for others it goes wrong from the first stroke. Add the complement and you lose chroma faster than you lose lightness.
"A complementary pair is high contrast." Contrast in what? Orange and its opposite blue differ by about 8 points of lightness; yellow-green and violet by 55. See Hue, value and chroma.
"The afterimage proves which colours belong together." It proves the eye pairs them. Whether the pair belongs in your image is a question about area, chroma and the job — see How to choose colours.


Reading a complementary pair in an image

Name the two hues, then decide which definition is in play. Mixed on the surface, or set side by side?
Compare their lightness by squinting. If one is clearly darker, that value gap is doing work you may be crediting to hue.
Compare their chroma. Two strong colours behave completely differently from one strong and one dull.
Estimate the area split. Near 50/50 is where complements fight; roughly 90/10 is where they read as field and accent.
If the pair sits at the same value and the same chroma with a hard edge between them, expect the boundary to buzz. That is a choice, and sometimes the right one.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              The colour wheel, and why there is more than one
              A ring of hues in spectral order, closed at the join by colours no wavelength can make. It is a working model, not a picture of light — and different jobs need different wheels, which is why they disagree about what sits opposite what.
            
          
        
          
            
              Hue, value and chroma
              A colour is not one thing. It is three independent dials — which colour it is, how light it is, and how far it sits from grey — and most arguments about colour are two people turning different dials.
            
          
        
          
            
              How to choose colours
              A practical order of operations for picking colours — decide the job, choose on all three dials, then set the areas — and an honest account of why the named schemes explain much less than they claim.
            
          
        
          
            
              The colour of the light
              What you see is the object's own colour multiplied by the light's colour — and your brain quietly divides the light back out, which is why a white shirt looks white everywhere.
